content: The document outlines a generic protocol designed for the development and maintenance of systematic reviews that evaluate interventions aimed at preventing pre-eclampsia and its associated complications. This protocol establishes a standardized methodology for selecting and assessing studies, developed in collaboration with existing review authors. The goal is to ensure a systematic and comprehensive approach to the topic, enhancing consistency across reviews and improving their readability and usability. Any significant deviations from this protocol in individual reviews will be explicitly stated. Unlike other protocols in The Cochrane Library, this generic protocol will not evolve into a full review but will remain permanently as a protocol. Reviews developed or updated using this protocol will be published separately in The Cochrane Library. Hypertension, or high blood pressure, is a common condition during pregnancy, affecting approximately 10% of women at some point before delivery. Pre-eclampsia, also known as toxaemia, is defined as hypertension accompanied by proteinuria (protein in the urine) and typically occurs in the second half of pregnancy, complicating 2% to 8% of pregnancies. For women with hypertension alone, pregnancy outcomes are generally similar to those with normal blood pressure. However, outcomes worsen once proteinuria develops. Mild pre-eclampsia is often asymptomatic, while severe pre-eclampsia or very high blood pressure can cause symptoms such as headache, upper abdominal pain, or visual disturbances. Pre-eclampsia can lead to complications in the liver, kidneys, brain, and clotting system. Rare but serious complications include eclampsia (seizures in a woman with pre-eclampsia), stroke, HELLP syndrome (haemolysis, elevated liver enzymes, and low platelets), and disseminated intravascular coagulation. These complications are associated with an increased risk of maternal death. The placenta is also involved in pre-eclampsia, increasing risks for the baby, including poor growth and premature birth. Although most women recover well after pre-eclampsia or eclampsia, these conditions remain significant causes of maternal mortality worldwide, with over half a million women dying annually from pregnancy-related causes, 99% of which occur in developing countries. Pre-eclampsia accounts for an estimated 10% to 15% of maternal deaths in developing countries and 13% to 15% of direct obstetric deaths in the UK and USA. Perinatal mortality is also elevated following pre-eclampsia, and morbidity for both mother and baby is likely high. Pre-eclampsia is part of a spectrum of hypertensive disorders of pregnancy, which exist on a continuum with normal pregnancy. During normal pregnancy, significant maternal physiological adaptations occur to support the growing fetus and placenta, such as a 40% increase in cardiac output during the first trimester. Blood pressure typically remains stable in the first trimester, decreases slightly in the second trimester, and returns to pre-pregnancy levels by term. Peripheral resistance decreases during normal pregnancy, and kidney function changes, including increased protein excretion, especially in the third trimester. Proteinuria up to 300 mg in 24 hours is considered normal during pregnancy. The classification and definitions of hypertensive disorders in pregnancy have historically been controversial, but there is now a consensus on standard definitions relevant to clinical practice. Hypertension in pregnancy is defined as a systolic blood pressure of at least 140 mmHg and/or a diastolic blood pressure of at least 90 mmHg, confirmed by a second measurement ideally taken at least four hours later. Blood pressure should be measured using an auscultatory device, as oscillometric techniques systematically under-record during pregnancy. Korotkoff phase V (disappearance of sound) is now recommended for assessing diastolic blood pressure, as it is more reliable. Proteinuria during pregnancy is defined as 300 mg or more of protein in 24 hours. This typically correlates with 30 mg/dL, 1+ or more on a dipstick, or a spot urine protein/creatinine ratio of at least 30 mg/mmol. Four main categories of hypertensive disorders in pregnancy are widely recognized: 1. Gestational Hypertension: Hypertension detected for the first time after 20 weeks of gestation without proteinuria, resolving within three months of birth. 2. Pre-eclampsia: Hypertension and proteinuria detected for the first time after 20 weeks of gestation. 3. Eclampsia: The occurrence of seizures in a woman with pre-eclampsia. 4. Chronic Hypertension: Hypertension present before pregnancy or detected before 20 weeks of gestation, which may be essential (no underlying cause) or secondary (due to renal, cardiac, or endocrine disease). Women with chronic hypertension may develop superimposed pre-eclampsia, diagnosed by new-onset proteinuria, sudden worsening of hypertension or proteinuria, or development of other signs and symptoms of pre-eclampsia after 20 weeks of gestation. Despite advances in understanding the pathophysiology of pre-eclampsia, its underlying cause remains unclear. Factors implicated include the placenta, maternal immune response, genetic predisposition, maternal vascular disease, and diet. The placenta plays a central role, as pre-eclampsia occurs only in the presence of a placenta, and its resolution begins with placental removal at delivery. Abnormal placental implantation and excessive placental tissue are key factors in the pathology of pre-eclampsia. Inadequate maternal immune adaptation to the fetus, which carries paternal genes, may also contribute, particularly in first pregnancies or pregnancies with a new partner. Pre-eclampsia tends to run in families, suggesting a genetic predisposition. Medical conditions associated with vascular disease, such as diabetes and chronic hypertension, increase the risk of pre-eclampsia. Thrombophilia, a group of conditions with a tendency for blood clotting, is associated with severe early-onset pre-eclampsia. Nutritional factors, such as calcium and fish oil intake, have been linked to pre-eclampsia risk, and dietary supplementation with magnesium, zinc, selenium, antioxidants, and folic acid has been suggested as preventive measures. Pre-eclampsia is thought to result from inadequate blood supply to the placenta, leading to the release of factors into the maternal circulation that cause endothelial dysfunction. This dysfunction results in widespread vasoconstriction, activation of platelets and the coagulation system, and reduced blood flow to maternal organs, causing the clinical manifestations of pre-eclampsia. Screening for women at risk of pre-eclampsia is an essential part of antenatal care. Current strategies for prevention focus on antenatal surveillance, lifestyle modification, nutritional supplementation, and pharmacological therapy. However, as the cause of pre-eclampsia is not fully understood and screening tests remain unreliable, developing rational prevention strategies is challenging.
